query: ("artificial intelligence" OR "generative AI" OR automation OR algorithm OR ChatGPT OR "large language model" OR robot OR "algorithmic management" OR "machine learning") AND (employee OR worker OR workplace OR job OR "future of work" OR occupation OR manager OR "human resource" OR workforce)

studies.headline: Worried AI will take your job? That anxiety may be quietly pushing you to manage your career better
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a three-wave, time-lagged survey of 329 full-time employees in the United Kingdom, measuring how aware workers were of AI's encroachment on their work, whether they experienced "impostor thoughts" at work, and how much they engaged in proactive career behaviors such as skill building, networking and career planning. AI awareness predicted more proactive career behavior, partly by way of feeling like an impostor. Crucially, that chain only held for employees with a vivid sense of their "future work self" — a clear mental picture of who they want to be professionally; for those without one, the impostor route went nowhere.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that technology-driven self-doubt converts into constructive career action only when people already have a concrete picture of where they are heading — otherwise it is just anxiety.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers rolling out AI tools may be inadvertently generating impostor feelings in their teams. The study hints that pairing AI adoption with explicit career-path conversations — helping people articulate what they want to be doing in three years — could channel that unease into reskilling rather than withdrawal; worth testing in your own team before assuming it works.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone feeling quietly inadequate as AI tools spread through their field: that feeling is common and measurable, and the people who seem to convert it into action are the ones who can describe the professional they want to become.
studies.caveats: Self-report survey from a single country; time-lagged but not experimental, so causation is not established, and the measures come from the same source at each wave. Proactive career behavior is self-reported rather than observed.
studies.paper_title: How and When Artificial Intelligence Awareness Fosters Proactive Career Behaviors: The Role of Workplace Impostor Thoughts and Future Work Self Salience

studies.headline: Workers managed by algorithms start treating customers as less than human
studies.the_study: A three-wave survey of 312 food delivery riders tested whether algorithmic management — automated task allocation, monitoring and scoring — changes how riders see the people they serve. Riders who experienced more algorithmic control were more likely to dehumanize customers, and that dehumanization predicted less customer-oriented behavior. Expressions of gratitude from customers weakened the link between algorithmic management and dehumanization.
studies.why_it_matters: Platforms optimizing service through tighter algorithmic control may be eroding the very thing they are optimizing for, and a simple human gesture from customers appears to buffer the effect.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your operation uses automated scoring, routing or monitoring, watch for a service-quality cost that does not show up in the dashboard: workers who feel processed by a system start processing other people the same way. Consider building moments of genuine human recognition into the workflow rather than relying on ratings alone.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Saying thank you to a delivery rider is not just politeness — in this data it was associated with riders holding on to a more human view of the customers they serve.
studies.caveats: Self-report across three waves, so direction of causation is uncertain; a single occupation (food delivery) and apparently a single national context; dehumanization and service behavior are worker-reported, not observed or customer-rated.
studies.paper_title: Dehumanized platform workers dehumanize customers: how algorithmic management reduces customer-oriented behavior

studies.headline: When the app decides who you are: how ratings and rankings rewrite gig workers' sense of worth
studies.the_study: Through interviews with delivery partners and platform managers in India, supplemented by multi-source data, researchers traced how algorithmic systems that allocate tasks, monitor performance and assign reputation scores in real time shape the identities workers adopt. They describe "algorithmic identity regulation": a continuous cycle of recognition, visibility and devaluation in which workers' sense of their own worth becomes contingent on algorithmic evaluation rather than on human judgment or professional standing.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows algorithmic management is not just a scheduling tool — it functions as a form of normative control that tells workers who they are supposed to become, with direct consequences for dignity at work.
studies.story_angle_primary: Any manager deploying continuous performance scoring should read this as a warning about what real-time, depersonalized feedback does to identity: recognition that is constant and datafied can feel less like recognition and more like surveillance. Ask whether your metrics leave room for human acknowledgment.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into the lived experience of the people who bring your dinner — and a preview of what work feels like when a score, not a supervisor, tells you how you are doing.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and interpretive; findings are not statistically generalizable. Single country (India) and single sector (food delivery platforms); no quantitative outcome measures.
studies.paper_title: Algorithmic identity regulation in the platform-based gig work of Indian food delivery workers

studies.headline: Actors, directors and screenwriters are improvising three very different responses to AI
studies.the_study: Forty semi-structured interviews with professionals in the Italian audiovisual industry — actors, directors, screenwriters, technicians and AI specialists — examined how creative workers interpret AI's effect on creativity, authorship and career. Analysis surfaced three forms of identity work: resisting (defending the human foundations of creativity), extending (embracing AI as a source of experimentation and new skills), and crafting (building a new professional identity around the human–AI boundary). Many participants reported identity ambiguity, with blurred lines between human originality, technological assistance and professional legitimacy.
studies.why_it_matters: In knowledge and creative occupations, the hardest part of AI adoption may not be learning the tool but renegotiating what makes you a professional at all.
studies.story_angle_primary: Leaders in creative, design and knowledge-work teams should expect resistance, enthusiasm and quiet reinvention to coexist in the same room — and recognize that the resisters are often defending a credential and a career identity, not just a workflow. Framing AI conversations around authorship and credit may do more than another training session.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone whose craft is becoming automatable: this is a map of the three stances people actually take, and why "just learn the tool" misses what is really at stake.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interviews with 40 people in one industry in one country (Italy); no measurement of outcomes such as earnings, employment or creative output; self-reported perceptions at a single point in time.
studies.paper_title: Negotiating professional identity in the creative industries: the REC framework for Human–AI creative work

studies.headline: Gig workers go the extra mile when the algorithm seems fair — but privacy monitoring backfires
studies.the_study: A three-wave time-lagged survey of 272 food delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers in China asked how workers judge the legitimacy of algorithmic management along three dimensions — autonomy, privacy and fairness — and how those judgments relate to proactive service behavior. Autonomy and fairness legitimacy predicted more proactive service, operating through autonomous motivation; privacy legitimacy was negatively related. Support from fellow workers actually weakened the motivational benefit of positive legitimacy judgments.
studies.why_it_matters: It indicates that how workers interpret an algorithm matters as much as what the algorithm does, and that perceived data intrusion is a distinct problem not fixed by making the system fairer.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you manage people through a platform or performance-tracking system, treat autonomy, fairness and privacy as three separate levers — this data suggests improving fairness will not offset the cost of feeling surveilled. Test transparency about what data is collected and why.
studies.story_angle_secondary: An unexpected finding for anyone who assumes workplace camaraderie is an unalloyed good: tight-knit peer communities seemed to dampen, not amplify, the motivating effect of believing the system is fair.
studies.caveats: Self-report survey across three waves, so causal claims are not warranted; single country (China) and two gig occupations; the counterintuitive peer-support moderation result is a single finding needing replication; outcome is self-reported behavior.
studies.paper_title: Legitimacy judgments of algorithmic management and gig workers' proactive service behavior: the roles of work motivation and colleague community support

studies.headline: Fifty years of Canadian census data: immigrants still earn less — and are concentrated in the wrong corners of the digital economy
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed Canadian Census microdata from 1971 to 2021, comparing earnings of immigrants and native-born workers across ten arrival cohorts, by gender and age at arrival, in six provinces. They also mapped 2021 industry employment against external measures of digital intensity and telework feasibility. Entry earnings gaps persist and cohort convergence remains incomplete, especially for women and recent arrivals; immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earning industries, and are underrepresented in high-earning, high-telework-feasibility sectors even though they are concentrated in many digitally intensive ones.
studies.why_it_matters: As remote-capable, high-paying work becomes the most prized segment of the labor market, this shows a structural sorting that education alone does not fix.
studies.story_angle_primary: For employers building hybrid and remote-eligible roles, the data flags a quiet equity risk: the jobs that got flexibility are not the jobs immigrant workers tend to hold. Auditing which of your roles are telework-eligible, and who holds them, is a concrete step.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A long-view answer to a question many newcomers ask: how long does it take to catch up? Across five decades of Canadian data, for many cohorts the answer is that full convergence never arrives.
studies.caveats: Descriptive and correlational census analysis, not causal; individual productivity, actual AI adoption, ICT use and remote-work uptake were not observed, so the digital-economy mapping is inferential and industry-level; findings are specific to Canada.
studies.paper_title: Immigrant earnings and labour-market positioning in a transforming digital labour market: evidence from Canada, 1971–2021

studies.headline: Letting AI make the final call on HR decisions damages a company's reputation
studies.the_study: Across three studies, researchers tested how outsiders judge organizations based on who holds final authority over consequential HR decisions — an AI system or a human HR specialist. When AI held the final say, external observers inferred that the company treated employees as objects rather than people, and that inference drove down the organization's reputation. The damage was smaller when the AI was perceived as more humanlike and larger when the HR issue at stake mattered more to the observer.
studies.why_it_matters: Companies racing to automate hiring, promotion and termination decisions may be buying efficiency at the cost of their employer brand and public standing — and the reputational hit comes specifically from handing AI the last word, not from using AI at all.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are deploying AI in HR, the design question that may matter most for reputation is not accuracy but authority: keeping a named human accountable for the final decision, and saying so publicly, is a cheap hedge worth testing. Watch how candidates, customers and journalists react to disclosure language about automated decisions.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The finding puts a name to a gut feeling many job seekers have — that being rejected by a machine says something about how a company sees people. It suggests that public discomfort with algorithmic HR is less about technical competence than about being treated as a data point.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies with external observers judging described scenarios rather than real hiring or firing decisions; outcomes are reputation perceptions, not actual business consequences; sample details and whether online panels were used are not specified in the abstract.
studies.paper_title: When AI Makes Final Decisions: The Effects of HR Decision Authority Within AI ‐Enabled HRM on Organizational Reputation

studies.headline: Workers who see AI coming are less likely to do the career work that would protect them
studies.the_study: A three-wave survey of 341 full-time employees tested how a vivid sense of one's "future work self" translates into feeling employable. Employees with a clearer future work self engaged in more career crafting — proactively shaping their work, skills and networks — which in turn raised perceived employability. But awareness of smart technologies, AI, robotics and algorithms (STARA) weakened that chain: the more employees saw technology disrupting their field, the less their career ambitions converted into proactive career behavior.
studies.why_it_matters: The people most alert to AI disruption appear to be the ones whose career initiative stalls, which is the opposite of what reskilling policy assumes.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers running AI-transition communications should watch for a chilling effect: messaging that emphasizes how much technology will change the job may dampen, rather than spark, the self-directed development they want. Pair disruption talk with concrete, visible paths forward and test whether career crafting actually goes up.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For individuals, the study suggests a trap worth naming: anxiety about AI can make a clear picture of your future career feel pointless, so you stop acting on it. Having a vision is only useful if it survives contact with the headlines.
studies.caveats: Self-report survey across three waves with the same source for predictors and outcomes; perceived employability is a perception, not actual job-market outcomes; sample occupation and country are not specified in the abstract; moderation effects of this kind are typically small.
studies.paper_title: Seeing the future or losing it? The roles of STARA awareness and career crafting in shaping perceived employability

studies.headline: People accept AI as a subordinate but not as a boss — and the sticking point is morality, not competence
studies.the_study: Researchers systematically reviewed 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering and computer science on how people evaluate algorithms, virtual agents and robots occupying organizational roles. A consistent pattern emerged: artificial agents in leader roles are seen as a poor fit, driven largely by perceived deficits in fairness, trustworthiness and other moral attributes rather than by doubts about their competence. Agents in follower roles are judged as fitting expectations, while teammate and partner roles depend on task context and design cues such as appearance and voice.
studies.why_it_matters: It pinpoints exactly where resistance to AI authority comes from, which tells organizations that making an AI system smarter will not make people willing to be led by it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before assigning AI to allocate work, evaluate people or set direction, consider that the resistance you will face is moral rather than technical — demonstrations of accuracy will not resolve it, while transparency, appeal rights and a human who owns the judgment might. AI in a supporting or executing role draws far less friction.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The review explains why an algorithm scheduling your shifts feels different from an algorithm suggesting your playlist: people grant machines competence readily but withhold the trust and sense of fairness they expect from someone with power over them.
studies.caveats: A synthesis of existing studies rather than new data, and the underlying evidence base is described as mixed; many constituent studies are likely lab or scenario-based with student or online samples; the integrative model itself is conceptual and untested.
studies.paper_title: Artificial Agents as Leaders and Followers: An Integrative Role-Congruity Review

fact_check.headline: Worried AI will take your job? That anxiety may be quietly pushing you to manage your career better
fact_check.notes: Design, N, country and the moderated-mediation pattern all match the abstract; causal language is appropriately hedged and caveats are complete.

fact_check.headline: Workers managed by algorithms start treating customers as less than human
fact_check.notes: Facts (three waves, 312 riders, gratitude moderator) match. Headline asserts causation that a correlational three-wave survey cannot support, though the caveat acknowledges it.

issues.label: Causal headline for correlational survey
issues.as_written: Workers managed by algorithms start treating customers as less than human
issues.abstract_says: Our findings suggest that algorithmic management is positively associated with workers' dehumanization of customers, whereas their dehumanization of customers is negatively associated with customer-oriented behavior.
issues.problem: The abstract reports associations from a three-wave self-report survey; the headline states a causal process ("start treating"), which the design cannot establish even though the caveat notes the limitation.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to an associational claim, e.g. "Workers who feel managed by algorithms are more likely to see customers as less than human".

fact_check.headline: When the app decides who you are: how ratings and rankings rewrite gig workers' sense of worth
fact_check.notes: Qualitative design, participants (delivery partners and platform managers in India), multi-source data and the dignity/identity-regulation argument are all faithfully represented, with appropriate caveats on generalizability.

fact_check.headline: Actors, directors and screenwriters are improvising three very different responses to AI
fact_check.notes: 40 interviews, Italian audiovisual industry and the resist/extend/craft framework are accurate; one quantifier ("many participants") is not supported by the abstract.

issues.label: Unsupported quantifier
issues.as_written: Many participants reported identity ambiguity, with blurred lines between human originality, technological assistance and professional legitimacy.
issues.abstract_says: More critically, AI also generates identity ambiguity and fragmentation, blurring boundaries between human originality, technological assistance, and professional legitimacy.
issues.problem: The abstract presents identity ambiguity as a thematic finding, not as something counted across "many participants"; the proportion is unverifiable from the abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to "The analysis also surfaced identity ambiguity, with blurred lines between...".

fact_check.headline: Gig workers go the extra mile when the algorithm seems fair — but privacy monitoring backfires
fact_check.notes: Sample and design are correct, but the headline and takeaway reinterpret the negative privacy-legitimacy coefficient as evidence that surveillance harms motivation — the opposite of what the variable measures. Mediation is also simplified to one pathway.

issues.label: Reinterpretation reverses the measured variable
issues.as_written: It indicates that how workers interpret an algorithm matters as much as what the algorithm does, and that perceived data intrusion is a distinct problem not fixed by making the system fairer.
issues.abstract_says: Autonomy legitimacy and fairness legitimacy were positively related to proactive service behavior, whereas privacy legitimacy was negatively related.
issues.problem: Privacy legitimacy is workers' judgment that the system's handling of privacy is legitimate; a negative relationship means higher privacy legitimacy went with less proactive service, not that perceived intrusion reduces it. The headline ("privacy monitoring backfires") and the manager angle ("improving fairness will not offset the cost of feeling surveilled") invert the direction of the measured construct.
issues.suggested_fix: State the finding as the abstract does — judging the algorithm legitimate on privacy grounds was associated with *less* proactive service, an unexplained counterintuitive result — and drop the "surveillance backfires" framing.

issues.label: Mediation simplified
issues.as_written: Autonomy and fairness legitimacy predicted more proactive service, operating through autonomous motivation
issues.abstract_says: Autonomous and controlled motivation served as distinct mediating mechanisms.
issues.problem: The abstract reports two distinct mediating pathways; the digest mentions only autonomous motivation.
issues.suggested_fix: Note that both autonomous and controlled motivation acted as distinct mediators, with peer support moderating only the autonomous pathway.

fact_check.headline: Fifty years of Canadian census data: immigrants still earn less — and are concentrated in the wrong corners of the digital economy
fact_check.notes: Data source, period, cohorts and provinces are accurate and caveats cover the unobserved variables; two small overreaches on scope and on "never" converging.

issues.label: Positioning result applies to two cohorts only
issues.as_written: immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earning industries
issues.abstract_says: For two recent cohorts, an earnings-based positioning measure combines industry mean annual earnings with full-time or part-time status... Across the two positioning cohorts, immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earnings industries
issues.problem: The digest presents a result limited to two recent arrival cohorts as if it applied across all ten cohorts analyzed.
issues.suggested_fix: Add "for the two most recent arrival cohorts analysed".

issues.label: "Never arrives" overstates incomplete convergence
issues.as_written: Across five decades of Canadian data, for many cohorts the answer is that full convergence never arrives.
issues.abstract_says: Entry earnings gaps and incomplete cohort convergence persist, especially among women and recent cohorts.
issues.problem: "Incomplete convergence" within the observation window is not the same as convergence never occurring; the abstract makes no claim about the eventual endpoint.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "for many cohorts, convergence remains incomplete across the period observed".

fact_check.headline: Letting AI make the final call on HR decisions damages a company's reputation
fact_check.notes: The objectification mechanism and both moderators are reported correctly; the design label "experimental" is not stated in the abstract, though the digest flags that sample details are missing.

issues.label: Design label not in abstract
issues.as_written: Experimental studies with external observers judging described scenarios rather than real hiring or firing decisions
issues.abstract_says: Across three studies, we show that when AI rather than human HR specialists holds final decision authority over consequential HR decisions, external stakeholders infer greater employee objectification, which, in turn, damages organizational reputation.
issues.problem: The abstract says only "three studies"; whether they were experiments with scenario vignettes is unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "three studies whose designs and samples are not specified in the abstract" rather than asserting scenario experiments.

fact_check.headline: Workers who see AI coming are less likely to do the career work that would protect them
fact_check.notes: N, waves and the mediation chain are correct, but the headline and "Why it matters" convert a moderation (STARA awareness weakens the future-work-self → career-crafting link) into a main effect of STARA awareness on career behavior.

issues.label: Moderation presented as a main effect
issues.as_written: Workers who see AI coming are less likely to do the career work that would protect them
issues.abstract_says: STARA awareness weakens the positive relationship between future work self and career crafting, thereby reducing the indirect effect of future work self on perceived employability.
issues.problem: The abstract reports only that STARA awareness attenuates the future-work-self→career-crafting path; it does not report that higher STARA awareness lowers career crafting overall. The headline, and the line "The people most alert to AI disruption appear to be the ones whose career initiative stalls," assert a direct negative effect that is not in the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe as conditional, e.g. "When workers see AI coming, a clear picture of their future career stops translating into career-building action".

fact_check.headline: People accept AI as a subordinate but not as a boss — and the sticking point is morality, not competence
fact_check.notes: Review scope (107 studies, four disciplines) and the leader/follower/partner pattern match the abstract; the "not competence" contrast is a small extrapolation beyond "driven largely by" morality deficits.

issues.label: "Not competence" overstated
issues.as_written: driven largely by perceived deficits in fairness, trustworthiness and other moral attributes rather than by doubts about their competence
issues.abstract_says: Artificial agents in leader roles face role incongruity, driven largely by perceived deficits in morality (e.g., fairness, trustworthiness).
issues.problem: The abstract says morality deficits are the main driver but does not rule competence out — indeed the AARC model retains a task dimension including competence. The digest's exclusive contrast, repeated in the headline and the advice that "demonstrations of accuracy will not resolve it," goes beyond the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Say morality-related perceptions are the dominant driver, without asserting that competence plays no role.

sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** Across this batch, worker and public resistance to AI at work is not about whether machines are capable — it is about who holds final authority and what being judged by a system does to a person's sense of worth. "People accept AI as a subordinate but not as a boss" (W7168435596) locates the objection in perceived fairness and trustworthiness rather than competence; "Letting AI make the final call on HR decisions damages a company's reputation" (W7204855159) shows outsiders punish firms specifically for handing AI the last word; and the gig studies — "When the app decides who you are" (W7213334889), "Workers managed by algorithms start treating customers as less than human" (W7218741843) and "Gig workers go the extra mile when the algorithm seems fair — but privacy monitoring backfires" (W7204647820) — show what happens downstream when a score, not a person, does the judging, including service quality that degrades in ways no dashboard captures.

**Why pitch this now:** Employers are embedding AI into hiring, scheduling, evaluation and termination just as human-oversight requirements for algorithmic management and high-risk employment systems move from debate into compliance deadlines, and most organizations are still treating this as an accuracy problem rather than an authority problem.

**Angle:** A reported feature arguing that the design decision with the biggest payoff in AI-era management is also the cheapest — naming a human who owns the final call and saying so out loud — written for executives, HR leaders and the workers on the receiving end, with gig platforms as the live experiment in what happens when nobody does.

**Potential headlines:**
- Workers Will Take Orders From Software — Until It Starts Deciding Their Fate
- The Problem With Your AI Isn't That It's Wrong
- When a Score Decides Your Worth, Something Breaks That No Metric Catches

**Potential outlets:**
- *MIT Sloan Management Review* — its readers are actively designing AI governance, and this is a concrete design principle (authority, not accuracy) backed by a 107-study review and experimental reputation data.
- *Harvard Business Review* — fits its appetite for evidence-based management arguments that overturn an executive assumption, here that better models will resolve resistance to algorithmic authority.
- *Wired* — strong track record on algorithmic management and platform labor; the India and China gig findings give the piece reported texture beyond the corporate layer.
- *The Atlantic* — the dignity-and-dehumanization thread, including riders who start seeing customers as less than human, is the kind of moral argument about work its readers follow.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **Worried AI will take your job? That anxiety may be quietly pushing you to manage your career better (Work ID W7223279808):** Impostor feelings triggered by AI only convert into skill building for people who can describe the professional they want to become — a usable test for anyone stuck in low-grade AI dread, for a career-advice column or a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest or women's/lifestyle outlet.
- **Workers managed by algorithms start treating customers as less than human (Work ID W7218741843):** Tighter algorithmic control was linked to riders dehumanizing customers and delivering worse service, with customer gratitude buffering the effect — a service-quality cost that never appears on the platform dashboard, for a manager-audience column or an operations/consumer news brief.
- **When the app decides who you are: how ratings and rankings rewrite gig workers' sense of worth (Work ID W7213334889):** Real-time scoring functions as identity control, not just scheduling, making workers' self-worth contingent on the algorithm — a strong narrative piece on dignity at work, for a general-interest feature section or a labor explainer.
- **Actors, directors and screenwriters are improvising three very different responses to AI (Work ID W7220851400):** Resist, extend, or craft a new identity on the human–AI boundary — a field guide to the three stances creative and knowledge workers actually take, and why "just learn the tool" lands badly, for a culture-and-work feature or a leadership column on managing creative teams.
- **Gig workers go the extra mile when the algorithm seems fair — but privacy monitoring backfires (Work ID W7204647820):** Fairness and autonomy motivate, surveillance does not, and improving one will not offset the other — three separate levers for anyone managing through tracking software, for an HR/management explainer, with the odd peer-support finding as a secondary hook.
- **Fifty years of Canadian census data: immigrants still earn less — and are concentrated in the wrong corners of the digital economy (Work ID W7222280836):** Immigrant workers cluster in digitally intensive industries but not the high-earning, telework-feasible ones, making remote flexibility a quiet new axis of inequality — for a business or policy news feature, or an HR explainer on auditing which roles are remote-eligible and who holds them.
- **Letting AI make the final call on HR decisions damages a company's reputation (Work ID W7204855159):** The reputational hit comes from AI holding final authority, not from using AI at all — meaning disclosure language and a named human decision-maker are cheap employer-brand insurance, for a hiring/HR explainer or a management column.
- **Workers who see AI coming are less likely to do the career work that would protect them (Work ID W7213541995):** Employees most alert to AI disruption showed weaker follow-through from career ambition to proactive action — a direct challenge to reskilling messaging built on urgency, for a workplace news brief or an L&D-focused management column; pairs sharply with W7223279808 as a point-counterpoint.
- **People accept AI as a subordinate but not as a boss — and the sticking point is morality, not competence (Work ID W7168435596):** A 107-study synthesis showing resistance to AI authority is about fairness and trust, not capability, so transparency and appeal rights matter more than model performance, for a manager-audience column or a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet.
